newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy parliament approves telecoms watchdog.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy parliament approves telecoms watchdog.

text.p: The Italian parliament on Tuesday approved a controversial bill to create a watchdog body to oversee the telecommunications and television sectors.

The much-delayed law opens the way for the privatisation later this year of state-controlled telecoms group Telecom Italia and ends months of bitter argument over the future development of Italy's lucrative television market.

Italy's upper house of parliament (Senate) gave the final go-ahead to the bill, with government parties in the centre-left Olive Tree coalition supporting the package and the centre-right opposition grouped in the Freedom Alliance abstaining.
"I'm very satisfied," Telecommunications Minister Antonio Maccanico told reporters after the vote, which was carried out by a show of hands.
"We have approved a very important bill which is in line with European Union directives and puts Italy at the forefront of the European telecoms sector," he added.

Under the terms of the law, a broadcasting and telecoms regulatory authority will be set up in September. The watchdog's chairman will be appointed by Prime Minister Romano Prodi, while parliament will elect the eight other members.

Legislation covering a watchdog body for the telecoms market has spent years crawling through parliament, with opponents to the privatisation process using the draft law as an opportunity to delay the long-awaited sale of Telecom Italia.
When Prodi's government took office in 1996 it decided to group television regulatory duties with the telecom market.

Prodi convinced hard-left allies Communist Refoundation about the need for the Telecom sell-off, but struggled to reach agreement with the centre-right opposition, headed by media mogul Silvio Berlusconi, over the issue of TV reform.
A compromise deal was finally struck earlier this month with some of the more sensitive issues put off to a later date.
Under the terms of the new law, no single television company will be allowed to control more than 20 percent of television broadcasting nor more than 30 percent of revenues.

Mediaset, which is controlled by Berlusconi, will be allowed to carry on operating three terrestrial channels, but the watchdog authority will eventually have to set a date to switch one of these to satellite transmission.
At the same time, state broadcaster RAI will have to stop using money from advertising to fund one of its three channels and rely soley on licence fees.
In addition, the authority faces the difficult task of re-allocating frequencies for Italy's plethora of TV companies.
The legislation also sets out a clear framework for the creation of a single digital pay TV system for Italy.

Mediaset, RAI, Telecom Italia, French broadcaster Canal Plus and its majority owned pay-TV, Telepiu, as well as Cecchi Gori Communications, announced on Monday that they would work together on the single platform.
But the first concrete result of the new law will be the privatisation of Telecom Italia, expected to be the largest flotation ever undertaken in Italy.
The sell-off, dubbed the mother of all privatisations, is planned for October and the government has already passed a decree covering technical aspects of the sale.
